catalog_quote: A palavra fonológica Máku é individualizada pelo conjunto juntura-acento, e também, pela sua distribuição no grupo de pausa. As fronteiras entre palavras fonológicas atualizam-se em junturas externas abertas. Cada palavra é também caracterizada pelo acento primário, não fonêmico [ ´ ] que cai sempre na última sílaba excetuado quando a palavra termina com o sufixo /-na/ nominalizador. Neste último caso, o acento cai na penúltima sílaba. Em palavras de três sílabas, a primeira sílaba recebe um acento secundário [ ]. Palavras com quatro e cinco sílabas recebem o acento secundário na segunda sílaba. As palavras fonológicas Máku são constituídas de uma sílaba ou combinação de duas, três, quatro ou cinco sílabas. ... /une/ [o:né] mãe /line/ [li:né] pedra, /eline/ [è:liné] a tua pedra, /ikilo/ [ì:kiló] caminho, /kuskexa/ [kù:skešá] está vendo. new_statements.translation: Each word is also characterized by the primary stress, non-phonemic [ ´ ], which always falls on the last syllable except when the word ends with the nominalizer suffix /-na/. In this latter case, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. In words of three syllables, the first syllable receives a secondary stress [ ` ]. Words with four and five syllables receive the secondary stress on the second syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable (non-contrastive) and falls on the final syllable of the phonological word; the only stated exception is words ending in the nominalizer suffix /-na/, which are stressed on the penult (i.e. /-na/ is extrametrical/unstressable). Examples: [o:né] 'mother', [i:kiló] 'path', [kù:skešá] 'is seeing'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of trisyllabic words and on the second syllable of four- and five-syllable words; a word-initial V (rarely CV) syllable bearing secondary stress is nearly as long as a long vowel in non-rapid speech.
new_statements.exceptions: Words ending in nominalizer /-na/ take penultimate stress. Author also notes some disyllables in pause-group-final position show tonal characteristics that 'seem distinctive' at a level above the phonological word (not analysed further). Migliazza 1978:134 adds /a/ is raised in unstressed position in casual speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'palavra fonológica' (phonological word), which the author says does not always coincide with the morphological word; word boundaries realized as open external junctures within the pause group. Based on elicited words/texts from the last 3 speakers (1964).
new_statements.identity_note: Migliazza 1965 describes the Máku of the upper Uraricuera and Uaris (Auari) rivers, Território de Roraima, from the last three speakers (fieldwork 1964; principal consultant Sinfrônio/Kuluta) — this is exactly Glottolog maku1246 'Máku' (a.k.a. Máku of Auari, Makú), NOT the Nadahup ('Makú') family nor Sapé/Arutani 'Maku'. The same speaker's data underlie Rogers 2020 and Zamponi 2026.
